title: EU sanctions draft would bar Russian flag and team athletes from events in Europe, including table tennis
seo_title: EU sanctions draft: what it means for Russians in table tennis
description: A leaked EU sanctions draft would bar athletes competing for Russia from events in the EU. What it could mean for WTT Contenders, Feeders and clubs.
standfirst: The draft would allow Russians to play only as neutrals at events on EU territory, from the Singles World Cup in Montpellier to Contenders, Feeders and possibly club matches.
body: A leaked draft of new European Union sanctions would bar athletes competing for Russia from sporting events held on EU territory, a rule that could reach table tennis from the Singles World Cup in Montpellier in March to Contenders, Feeders and club matches across the bloc. The draft would still let Russians play under a neutral status, and the Mixed Team World Cup in Chengdu, where Russia take their flag on Sunday, is outside its reach.

EUobserver reported on Wednesday that it had seen a draft 22nd package of sanctions on Russia. It says the text would let Russian athletes compete "under a neutral status", the only exemption it names, and would stop organisers, promoters and athletes displaying "official symbols of the Russian Federation, including flags, emblems, colours, anthems". Russian government officials could not enter venues in their formal capacities, and Russian nationals could not hold posts in international or national sports governing bodies established in an EU country. The outlet said the text could still change. It needs the agreement of all member states, including Slovakia and Bulgaria, which have vetoed EU culture sanctions before.
## What it would change in table tennis

The International Table Tennis Federation (ITTF) decided in July that athletes with Russian passports could return to its events from 28 July, in team as well as individual events, on the ordinary conditions that apply to everyone. It said the decision was subject to visas, sanctions and the law of host countries, which is the gap the EU draft would fill. Eleven's [feature on Russia's return](/news/russia-return-table-tennis-ittf-ban.html) set out how the ITTF followed the International Olympic Committee in both directions.

Since the flag came back, Russians have played at four WTT events in EU countries, according to Eleven's results database. Vladimir Sidorenko, the world No 19, played WTT Champions Montpellier and WTT Champions Frankfurt, and he, Elizabet Abraamian and Nikita Artemenko played Europe Smash in Malmö in August, where Russians competed under their own flag. Mariia Tailakova played WTT Contender Panagyurishte in Bulgaria in September. Under the draft, any of those entries would have to be neutral, with no flag, anthem or colours.

The lower WTT tiers are where Russia's depth shows. Russians have played Contenders in Almaty and Istanbul this year, and the only Feeder in Eleven's results with Russian players since 28 July is Tashkent, outside the EU. The 2027 calendar has several Contenders and Star Contenders inside the bloc: WTT Contender Lille from 2 to 7 February, WTT Star Contender Ljubljana from 8 June, WTT Contender Zagreb from 17 August, WTT Contender Panagyurishte from 30 August and WTT Star Contender Germany from 9 November. WTT Feeders are played across Europe too, such as WTT Feeder Düsseldorf II this week. The draft applies to where an event takes place, not its level, so a ban would cover each of them.

Slovenia has already shown what that looks like. Ljubljana let Russian players into the European Championships in October on condition that no Russian flag or anthem appeared, so when Abraamian won the women's title the ceremony had neither. The European Table Tennis Union (ETTU) said it had been obliged to apply the host's terms.

The draft's wording covers athletes who compete "on behalf of" Russia, and the report does not say whether Russians playing for European clubs would count. If they did, the effect would be large. Eleven's squad files list 11 Russian players across six clubs in the ETTU Champions League women's competition, in Germany, France, Italy, the Czech Republic and Spain. Sidorenko and Lev Katsman play for GV Hennebont in the French Pro A and the men's Champions League. The Champions League Final 4s are in Metz on 1 and 2 May for the women and in Saarbrücken on 8 and 9 May for the men. Nothing in the report suggests club players are targeted, and the final text would have to settle it.

The governance clause raises a second question. The ITTF is based in Lausanne, Switzerland, and EUobserver said Bern had not answered whether Switzerland would copy the ban. The Swiss foreign ministry and the International Olympic Committee did not reply to the outlet. Eleven found no statement from the ITTF, WTT or the ETTU on the draft.

EUobserver said the package faces a Brussels summit on Thursday, with pressure on Slovakia and Bulgaria to agree. The European Commission proposed the sports measures on Monday, and its president, Ursula von der Leyen, said then that sports events cannot be a forum for propaganda activities. If the package passes in anything like its present form, Russian players would still be able to enter EU events as neutrals, but not with their flag. The Mixed Team World Cup starts in Chengdu on Sunday.
